thread.title: Geometric Circle Covering Theorem
thread.preview:
Yes—I ran it using the **actual 5,986 Manhattan pickups**.

| Method | Load imbalance (CV)¹ | RMS assignment distance |
|---|---:|---:|
| Initial honeycomb allocation | 134.6% | 392 m |
| Your pooled-centroid rule | 119.8% | 373 m |
| Ordinary k-means, 100 centers | 76.1% | 226 m |

Your rule reached a fixed point after **25 sweeps**: no further movement or reassignment.

One important limitation: this Manhattan-shaped honeycomb patch had **70 boundary vertices fixed and only 30 interior vertices movable**. It ended with 26 empty regions, including 25 at the boundary. K-means allowed all centers to move, starting from the same layout and relocating empty centers.

So the rule improved both measurements modestly, but **convergence did not produce balanced loads**. Moving toward a pooled centroid provides no explicit pressure toward equal counts.

¹ CV = standard deviation of region loads divided by their mean; lower is better.

Keep boundary vertices fixed. Compare load imbalance and RMS assignment distance against the initial allocation and k-means. Use the actual pickup coordinates in the archive.

OK, I got a bit lost.  In what sense what we do is different from distributed k-means?

items.text:
The main difference is **what we optimize**. “Distributed” describes how agents coordinate.

| | Standard k-means | Our disk model |
|---|---|---|
| Assignment | Each dot belongs to its nearest center | Weight is split among covering disks; uncovered dots go to the nearest center |
| Objective | Minimize total squared distance to centers | Balance loads while limiting intersections |
| Variables | Center positions | Center positions **and radii** |
| Constraints | No overlap graph required | Connected disk graph, degree ≤6 |

**K-means does not aim for equal cluster loads.** Dense clusters can contain many more dots than sparse ones.

Our latest strict self-improvement and neighbor-annealing rules are also experimental choices, not standard k-means updates.

If we remove the disks and assign every dot to its nearest center, then seek balanced loads while keeping distances small, we are moving toward **balanced or capacity-constrained k-means**. That may be the simpler comparison to focus on.

Tested on **5,986 dots and 100 disks**, retaining the last move rule.

All three temperatures preserved connectivity, degree ≤6, and assigned every dot. **None reached 10% balance after 200,000 proposals**; the best final worst imbalance was **141%**.

A new issue emerged: **nearest-center assignments can change loads of non-intersecting disks**, so checking only intersection neighbors misses some harm.
